☆ Separating mixtures of single-fiber orientation distributions for increased sensitivity to crossing white matter fibers
Adam M. Saunders, Gaurav Rudravaram, Michael E. Kim, Elyssa M. McMaster, Yifan Shuai, Warren Boschen, Sophie Lin, Suzana Herculano-Houzel, Daniel C. Colvin, Yurui Gao, Kurt G. Schilling, Adam W. Anderson, Bennett Landman
Intro: Diffusion MRI allows for in vivo probing of brain tissue architecture via micron-level diffusion aggregated at the millimeter scale, but crossing white matter fibers decrease the sensitivity of downstream tasks such as microstructural modeling and tractography. Current fixel-based methods for identifying the number, orientation, and spread of fibers rely on finding the peaks of fiber orientation distributions from constrained spherical deconvolution. However, this method is biased by the spreads of nearby fibers and fails at angular separations lower than approximately 40-50 degrees. Methods: In this work, we perform a constrained nonlinear optimization called fiber segmentation by signal splitting and iterative least squares estimation (FISSILE), modeling each voxel as a mixture of single-fiber distributions. We use FISSILE to fit axially symmetric fibers in simulations and on three in vivo human subjects from the Human Connectome Project, an ex vivo raccoon brain, as well as the same human subject scanned twice at two different signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). Results: On simulated data, FISSILE successfully identifies fibers at an angular separation of 40° and a volume fraction of 0.1 at an SNR as low as 30, while MRtrix3's fod2fixel is limited to 60° separation and 0.1 volume fraction at the same SNR. On acquired data, FISSILE identified 85.8% of white matter voxels on average in human brains and 79.4% in the raccoon with at least one fiber crossing, whereas fod2fixel identified 30.1% and 44.5%. The number of white matter fiber crossings was mildly sensitive to different noise levels in the human subject with two acquisitions. Conclusion: A method that models the crossing fiber phenomenon as an unmixing problem increases sensitivity to individual fibers for more precise characterization of anatomy.

☆ A$^3$PreCore: Robust Rigid Registration for Native FLAIR-Space Brain-Mask Transfer
Elmira Mirzabeigi, Zahra Khalilzad, Taylor Snowden-Richardson, Jesus Eduardo Lugo Arce, Jodie R. Gawryluk, Brian R. Christie, Jocelyn Faubert
Reliable brain-mask transfer into native fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) space can fail when T1-to-FLAIR rigid registration is unstable. We developed A$^3$PreCore, a six-degree-of-freedom rigid-registration strategy that aligns the full bias-corrected T1-weighted image to native FLAIR using normalized mutual information while preserving the established T1-space anatomical mask. We also introduced extended quantitative quality control (E-QC), which characterizes mask extent, field-of-view-relative position, FLAIR intensity support, boundary support, inferior morphology, and pairwise geometric disagreement. In 78 participants with paired T1-weighted and FLAIR imaging, A$^3$PreCore was compared with fsl_anat and the Brain Extraction Tool (BET). Gross rigid-body misregistration occurred in 21/78 fsl_anat outputs (26.9%) and 0/78 A$^3$PreCore outputs (exact two-sided McNemar p=9.54 x 10^-7). Among 57 participants without gross fsl_anat misregistration, A$^3$PreCore preserved close agreement (median Dice=0.993; median paired Delta NMI=-0.00007, p=0.429). A$^3$PreCore remained broadly concordant with BET (median Dice=0.955), with less inferior and extracranial extension in representative comparisons. Method-blinded neuroscientists ranked A$^3$PreCore first in 35/40 participants (87.5%). E-QC additionally exposed severe orientation-related disagreement not evident from global descriptors or centroid displacement alone. These findings support A$^3$PreCore as a robust native-FLAIR brain-mask transfer strategy and E-QC as a complementary framework for multidimensional mask characterization and participant-specific geometric quality control.
☆ LightHybridNet: A Lightweight Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Efficient Multi-Label Ophthalmic Disease Classification in Imbalanced Fundus Images
Hem Raj Dadral Najam Ul Hasan, Naveed Ejaz, Muhammad Aslam Jarwar
Eye diseases are a major global cause of blindness and vision impairment, highlighting the need for accurate and early diagnosis to prevent further deterioration. Despite advances in medical imaging, classifying retinal diseases from fundus images remains challenging due to the complexity and subtlety of visual features. This study aims to develop and validate LightHybridNet, a novel lightweight hybrid deep learning framework, to improve the classification of eye diseases from fundus images. The model incorporates architectural features, such as depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling mechanisms, to enhance diagnostic accuracy and robustness. To validate the model, the ODIR-5K dataset, comprising 8 disease categories, was used. To enhance image quality, pre-processing approaches were applied, including histogram equalisation, colour space conversion, and contrast adjustment, resulting in high-resolution images. Furthermore, image augmentation was employed to increase the dataset size, thereby improving the model's ability to generalise during training. The hybrid architecture helps the model concentrate on relevant image regions while capturing and integrating details at different scales, significantly improving classification performance. To evaluate its effectiveness, the model was compared with transfer-learning models. The results show that LightHybridNet outperforms the baselines, achieving a weighted F1-score of 91.51%, a macro AUC of 98.26%, and a Cohen's Kappa of 90.14% on the validation set. Furthermore, model interpretability was enhanced using explainable AI methods, including Grad-CAM, to identify and emphasise features influencing the decision-making process. LightHybridNet represents a promising advancement in automated ocular disease detection, offering improved diagnostic reliability for clinical use.
♻ ☆ BOLT: Universal Classifier Training via a Bayes-Error Upper Bound
Mohammadreza Tavasoli Naeini, Ali Bereyhi, Morteza Noshad, Ben Liang, Alfred O. Hero
This work introduces a novel approach to compute a universal upper bound on the Bayes error rate (BER) from classifier-output samples, which serves as a Bayes-error-related performance criterion for the underlying classification task. We show that the bound is tight in the binary case and characterize the max-sum gap that appears in the aggregate multiclass formulation. Based on this bound, we define a new loss function, called Bayes optimal learning threshold (BOLT), for training parameterized classifiers. For each data sample, the BOLT loss computes a term whose expectation upper-bounds the Bayes error, so that during training the model parameters can be updated toward minimizing this bound. Numerical experiments with both synthetic and real-world datasets show that, in the reported settings, BOLT training often attains lower held-out classification error than cross-entropy training.
♻ ☆ Tile-Based Phase Unwrapping with Reliability-Ordered Joining and Residual-Weighted Multipath Averaging
Antoine Moevus, Max Mignotte
Phase unwrapping recovers a continuous phase map from measurements known only modulo 2π, in the presence of noise and discontinuities. We propose a tile-based method that combines local spectral reconstruction, reliability-ordered tile joining, and residual-weighted multipath averaging. Each tile is reconstructed by a discrete cosine transform (DCT) least-squares solve, and robust measurements along tile borders guide their joining along a spanning tree. We repeat this reconstruction on shifted tile grids and on rotated and reflected copies of the image, which changes tile borders and joining paths. A residual-weighted average combines the resulting reconstructions, which are computed in parallel and averaged on the fly without being stored. We also introduce the corrected circular rewrapping error, a congruence measure: after removing a global phase offset, it measures how far the rewrapped reconstruction is from the observed phase. It applies to least-squares and path-based methods, even without an unwrapped reference. Used with reference-based errors, it separates agreement with the measurement from recovery of the correct number of cycles. Experiments on radar-interferometric, magnetic-resonance, holographic, and constructed phase images compare our method with seven reference algorithms. Among the methods that complete every test image, ours has the lowest mean fraction of pixels with an error above π. On the images all methods complete, it lies on several speed-accuracy Pareto fronts. Error maps also reveal isolated cycle errors that average scores or congruence alone can hide.

♻ ☆ A comparative assessment of global building and settlement datasets across geographic and settlement contexts
Rufai Omowunmi Balogun, Caroline Margaux Gevaert, Capucine Riom, Derrick Mirindi, Aaron Opdyke, Hamed Alemohammad, Pierre Chrzanowski, Edward Charles Anderson
Global building and settlement products increasingly support population mapping, exposure assessment, and urban monitoring, yet comparative evidence remains fragmented across representations, geographic contexts, and evaluation methods. We benchmark seven global or near-global products against harmonized reference building footprints across 135 study areas. Our representation-aware framework integrates complementary measures of detection, geometric agreement, and aggregate quantity accuracy with stratified analyses of settlement characteristics, evaluation resolution, reference provenance, and temporal alignment. Overture Maps achieved the highest median city-level vector F1 (0.786), while 3D-GloBFP showed the closest aggregate building-area agreement despite weaker detection performance. Raster rankings were scale-dependent: Google Open Buildings Temporal (OBT) performed best at 10\,m (F1 = 0.680), whereas WSF Tracker led at 100\,m (F1 = 0.904) but substantially overestimated reference building area (relative bias = 1.845). Raster accuracy increased with building density ($ρ=0.58$--$0.75$), while smaller candidate footprints were disproportionately associated with vector false positives. Temporal alignment improved WSF Tracker mean city-level F1 by 0.060. These findings demonstrate that product reliability depends on representation, spatial scale, and settlement context, providing a reproducible framework for assessing the suitability of EO-derived urban information for different applications.
♻ ☆ Medical Imaging Classification with Cold-Atom Reservoir Computing using Auto-Encoders and Surrogate-Driven Training
Nuno Batista, Ana Morgado, Oscar Ferraz, Sagar Silva Pratapsi, Jorge Lobo, Gabriel Falcao
We introduce a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline, based on neutral-atom reservoir computing, for medical image classification, focusing on the binary classification task of polyp detection. To deal effectively with the high dimensionality, we integrate a guided auto-encoder. This pipeline learns compact and discriminative representations of image data that are also well-suited for quantum reservoir computing. A key challenge in such systems is the non-differentiable nature of quantum measurements, which creates a 'gradient barrier' for standard training. We overcome this barrier by incorporating a differentiable surrogate model that emulates the quantum layer, enabling end-to-end backpropagation through the entire system. This guided training process is jointly optimized for classification accuracy and for faithful image recovery from the auto-encoder. The learned latent representations are encoded as pulse detuning parameters within a Rydberg Hamiltonian, and quantum embeddings are subsequently obtained through expectation values. These embeddings are then passed to a linear classifier. Our simulations show that this method outperforms some traditional approaches that use PCA or unguided autoencoders. We also conduct ablation studies to assess the impact of various quantum and training parameters, demonstrating the robustness and flexibility of our proposed pipeline for real-world medical imaging applications, even in the current NISQ era.

♻ ☆ Synergistic Vision-Language Reinforcement Enables Scalable On-Demand Analysis across Diverse Clinical Tasks
Haonan Wang, Jiaji Mao, Lehan Wang, Qixiang Zhang, Marawan Elbatel, Yi Qin, Huijun Hu, Baoxun Li, Wenhui Deng, Weifeng Qin, Hongrui Li, Jialin Liang, Jun Shen, Xiaomeng Li
Accurate segmentation of tumors and organs-at-risk is essential for oncology but remains time-consuming and expertise-intensive. Existing AI systems often require manual spatial prompts or task-specific retraining, while generic class labels provide limited guidance for heterogeneous disease targets. Here we present SyRe, a text-prompted segmentation foundation model based on Synergistic vision-language Reinforcement, which strengthens bidirectional interaction between visual and linguistic representations. We introduce Color Region Description (CRD) to generate region-level semantic supervision and construct SyReData, comprising 20 million image-mask-description triplets across 9 modalities and 229 segmentation tasks. Training with diversified prompt formats enables single-target, multi-target and open-ended segmentation, together with invalid-prompt rejection. SyRe achieves accurate segmentation across diverse clinical scenarios, with strong gains on disease-related targets. Evaluation on 28 unseen external datasets, including 17 cancer types, 3 non-cancer diseases and multinational in-house cohorts, demonstrates generalization under distribution shift. Beyond spatial overlap, SyRe-generated masks preserve quantitative pathology information. Across five retrospective tumor imaging cohorts spanning CT and MRI, radiomics derived from these masks stratify survival and improve prognostic modeling over clinical baselines. Clinician-in-the-loop refinement further supports case-level correction. These results establish SyRe as a generalizable framework for scalable quantitative oncology analysis and clinician-guided segmentation.
♻ ☆ SCI-Mamba: Unsupervised Learning based Low-Light Image Enhancement for Non-Cooperative Spacecraft
Yiyong Sun, Weihang Shan, Shijun Wei, Diwei Zhou, Guang Zhai
Low-light visual perception acts as the core visual foundation for on-orbit servicing missions targeting non-cooperative spacecraft, supporting autonomous rendezvous, pose estimation, component detection and robotic capture operations. Spaceborne imagery suffers from severe low-light degradation, while the extreme scarcity of paired normal/low-light space samples severely limits the generalization capacity of supervised enhancement algorithms. To address this practical bottleneck, this paper proposes SCI-Mamba, an unsupervised enhancement network for low-light orbital spacecraft observations. The proposed framework unites self-calibrated unsupervised learning, linear-complexity VMamba architecture and Retinex physical priors, delivering a lightweight enhancement pipeline adaptable to resource-limited spaceborne hardware. We construct Space Dark-1.0, a dedicated low-light spacecraft dataset integrating real orbital footage, darkroom hardware-in-the-loop measurements and physically constrained synthetic data covering diverse illumination, motion and attitude conditions. Comprehensive comparisons with CNN-, Transformer- and prevailing Mamba-based approaches verify the advantages of SCI-Mamba in visual authenticity, color fidelity and inference speed. The proposed framework provides a practical low-light enhancement solution for close-proximity non-cooperative space operations. The code is available at https://github.com/bitswh/SCI-Mamba

☆ Deep Learning for Atmospheric Turbulence Mitigation: A Comparison Between GANs and Transformers
Juan S. Carrillo, Jérôme Gilles
Atmospheric turbulence creates complex spatial and temporal distortions that significantly reduce image quality. This work compares two deep learning methods for turbulence reduction: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Transformer-based models. Both methods are trained and tested on the SOTIS dataset, which includes multi-frame sequences under different turbulence conditions with ground truth references. Our results show an important finding: GAN-based models perform better in severely degraded, low-quality situations, while Transformer-based models achieve better results in moderate to high-quality settings, especially in correcting geometric distortions. We also enhance the Turbulence Mitigation Transformer (TMT) by introducing a refined training strategy, an augmented input design that includes a temporally averaged frame as prior structural information, and a modified loss function that incorporates the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM). These improvements lead to consistent performance gains across various turbulence conditions. Overall, this study provides an in-depth evaluation of deep learning methods for turbulence reduction and offers practical guidance for selecting models in different imaging environments.

☆ High-resolution retinal matrix imaging via computational motion and aberration correction
Aymeric Melt, Léo Puyo, Victor Barolle, Claude Boccara, Gereon Hüttmann, Alexandre Aubry
High-resolution optical imaging of the human retina is essential for diagnosing ophthalmic and neurodegenerative diseases. While adaptive optics combined with coherence gating can resolve retinal structures at the cellular scale, it requires complex, costly, and cumbersome hardware to physically correct for ocular aberrations and motion. Matrix imaging offers a powerful digital alternative by leveraging wave linearity to undo aberrations and multiple scattering; however, its in vivo deployment has been hindered by continuous, involuntary eye movements that destroy phase coherence during acquisition. Here, we overcome this fundamental barrier and demonstrate the first in vivo reflection matrix imaging of the human retina using an ultra-simplified optical setup without physical correctors. We introduce a fully computational framework that tracks and compensates for multi-axial ocular motion directly from raw interferometric data, thereby restoring the phase coherence of a multi-spectral distortion matrix. This enables local, high-order aberration correction to achieve diffraction-limited, volumetric imaging of retinal tissues. By shifting the hardware burden to physics-guided numerical computation, this paradigm opens the way for accessible, non-invasive, and high-resolution digital ophthalmology.

☆ Per-Bundle, Pre-Reconstruction Inversion for Temporal CT: Flux-Compensation Design and Multi-Patient Generalization
Guy M Besson
Paper 1 established the per-bundle statistical limits of Temporal CT (TCT) and benchmarked a learned prior on a single patient at a uniform incident count $N_0$. This paper lifts both restrictions. SNN2, a Gauss-Newton estimator, converges to the per-bundle Poisson maximum-likelihood solution and is the prior-free baseline. N$_0$FC, a bow-tie and tube-current-modulation co-design, compresses within-bundle photon-flux dynamic range. V8c is a neural-network residual corrector trained on a 19-patient corpus stratified by water-equivalent diameter (WED). T2bp, a per-patient empirical-Bayes post-processor, combines per-bundle Poisson likelihoods with a prior built from the patient's own bundles; it requires no training, so it cannot inherit a mismatched training prior. Results use Paper 1's bias-charged Dose Inflation Factor (DIF), extended to per-ray budgets. V8c beats SNN2 on in-distribution patients under baseline acquisition but fails out of distribution. Composed with SNN2, T2bp matches or beats T2bp$\circ$V8c on three of four N$_0$FC test cells (WED 207-342 mm), with the largest gains on the high-WED and out-of-distribution patients, and trails by 3% on the fourth. On 23 non-test corpus volumes, N$_0$FC with closed-loop tube-current modulation lowers the per-volume median middle-path Cramer-Rao floor, as a DIF, from 23-48 under baseline acquisition to 3.3-6.3, near the equal-attenuation value 13/3; T2bp$\circ$SNN2 reaches this floor without training, its mean squared error 0.74-1.26 times the floor (median 0.89) over the bulk of each volume. Acquisition co-design removes most of the attenuation-contrast penalty, and a training-free estimator attains the resulting limit. The remaining three- to six-fold gap to dose parity with single-source CT, and the high-attenuation tail, are the target of inter-bundle priors in later work.

☆ Perceptual Characterization of Scan-induced Artifacts in Dynamic 3D Meshes
Huong Hoang, Truong Nguyen, Pamela Cosman
Dynamic meshes reconstructed from real-world scenes often exhibit scan-induced artifacts such as surface jitter and missing geometry, which strongly impact perceived visual quality. Objective assessment remains challenging due to the absence of artifact-free ground truth and limited perceptual understanding of artifact interactions. This paper presents a systematic and controlled perceptual study of scan-induced artifacts in dynamic meshes, focusing on surface jitter and holes. To enable systematic analysis, we introduce a physically grounded artifact synthesis framework in which holes are synthesized using a reconstruction uncertainty model derived from multi-view geometry. The study reveals asymmetric cross-artifact interactions, non-additive integration, and motion-dependent temporal masking. Based on these findings, we propose a compact, perceptually grounded no-reference quality assessment framework that encodes the observed perceptual mechanisms.
☆ DoReMe: Dual optimization of Reconstruction and Motion estimation for self-navigated free-breathing abdominal MRI using Gaussian Splatting
Majd Helo, Dominik Nickel, Thomas Kuestner
Purpose: Free-breathing abdominal MRI is limited by respiratory motion, which introduces image artifacts and k-space inconsistencies. Existing reconstruction approaches often depend on pre-estimated motion fields or external respiratory surrogate signals. We propose a coupled reconstruction-motion estimation algorithm for self-navigated free-breathing acquisition, in which motion is represented by compact Gaussian primitives and jointly refined with the image estimates during iterative reconstruction. Methods: An iterative reconstruction that alternates between data consistency updates and motion modelling was proposed. Respiratory motion was represented using Gaussian primitives. A Gaussian splatting was integrated into the reconstruction algorithm. The method was evaluated on self-navigated free-breathing Cartesian gradient-echo (GRE) acquisition in four healthy volunteers, including retrospective scan shortening experiments, and was compared with regularized compressed sensing (CS) reconstruction. Results: Respiratory motion states were reconstructed in approximately 1.5 min. Compared with CS, the proposed method improved visual image quality, particularly in coronal liver views, and better preserved anatomical structures in retrospectively shortened acquisitions. These findings provide proof of concept for the proposed method. Conclusion: The proposed coupled reconstruction-motion estimation algorithm improved visual image quality compared with CS alone. Gaussian primitives provided a compact and sufficiently flexible representation of nonrigid respiratory motion with practical runtime, supporting further scanner integration and validation in larger cohorts.

☆ Focus, Align, and Diffuse: Time-Series-Aware Keyframe Diffusion for Cardiac Dynamic Synthesis from Sparse Observations NeurIPS 2026
Junkai Liu, Haofan Wu, Nay Aung, Joao A. C. Lima, Steffen E. Petersen, Le Zhang
Dense cardiac dynamics are essential for assessing cardiac function, yet in practice clinicians often observe only extremely sparse measurements. However, recovering full dynamics from such sparsity is a highly ill-posed problem due to the lack of temporal cues. While auxiliary time-series signals like ECG provide physiological guidance, effectively exploiting them is challenging due to the cross-modal representation gap and phase misalignment. In this work, we present CardioFAD, a Focus--Align--Diffuse paradigm that reformulates sparse cardiac dynamic synthesis as a recoverability--alignability anchor discovery problem. Our core insight is that resolving extreme temporal ambiguity requires a compact set of anchor states that are both sufficient to recover the visual trajectory and reliable for ECG--visual alignment. We therefore learn motion-salient keyframes under two complementary principles: trajectory sufficiency, which preserves trajectory-critical intra-modal motion content, and anchor alignment, which promotes consistent inter-modal correspondence at these anchors. We implement the Focus and Align modules optimized by the two aspects. Diffuse then performs two-stage generation by first synthesizing keyframes and subsequently interpolating the remaining frames. Extensive experiments on cardiac MRI and echocardiography videos demonstrate superior visual quality, temporal coherence, and improved functional consistency under the extreme one-shot regime.

☆ Simplifying and Improving On-Policy Distillation for Few-Step Diffusion
Jiawei Zhang, Ziyu Wan, Nanye Ma, Long Zhao, Dong Chen, Hongyu Liu, Qifeng Chen, Dongdong Chen
Few-step distillation reduces the sampling cost of diffusion and flow models, but existing approaches often require auxiliary score models or specialized architectures. We show that simple on-policy velocity regression already provides a strong foundation for 4-NFE generation. To represent teacher velocity variation within each coarse transition, we introduce Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that separates local corrections from the student's interval-mean prediction. We further repel the student from weaker teacher predictions, providing a lightweight mechanism for avoiding undesirable modes. The resulting framework, Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD), remains entirely regression-based, requires neither online score estimation nor adversarial training, and leaves the deployed generator unchanged. We evaluate SMD on image generation and editing, 3D generation, video synthesis, and joint audio--video generation, scaling to 33 billion parameters. At 4-NFE, SMD outperforms strong few-step baselines and surpasses multi-step teachers on several benchmarks. It also supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation.

☆ Augmenting Real-time Visualization in Minimally Invasive Surgery with Particle Filtering and Depth-Aware Occlusion Handling
Anuska Sarkar, Partha Acharya, Vishnu Nandury, Kaustav Basu, Subhamoy Mandal
We present a real-time, hybrid framework for occlusion handling and depth-aware tracking in minimally invasive surgeries (MIS). Occlusions caused by surgical instruments often obscure the region of interest (ROI), affecting surgical precision. To address this, our approach integrates enhanced You Only Look Once (YOLO) based detection, Particle Filtering (PF), and monocular depth estimation using Multiple Depth Estimation Accuracy with Single Network (MiDaS). Occlusion is detected using a distance-based threshold between instruments and ROI. Experimental results demonstrate robust instrument detection with a confidence score of 0.85, effective occlusion event handling, and accurate depth prediction with an MAE of 0.34 cm and RMSE of 0.53 cm. Independent phantom-based validation against stereo depth measurements yielded an MAE of 0.65 cm and RMSE of 0.66 cm. The framework further achieved an occlusion detection accuracy of 81.95\% while maintaining real-time performance at 38.7 FPS. Preliminary surgeon feedback indicates that the proposed visualization framework is clinically relevant and holds promise for future intraoperative image-guided navigation and decision support in MIS.

☆ Recovery-Oriented Optical System Design Based on Fisher Information
Zhuang Qian, Yan Mo, Hao Tan, Yu Chen, Haibo Wang, Weining Guo, Yijie Ni, Donglin Ma
Traditional optical system design for imaging applications has long been guided by image quality metrics such as geometrical RMS spot size, wavefront error, and modulation transfer function (MTF). Although these metrics effectively characterize direct imaging performance, they do not necessarily indicate optimal behavior when image restoration is subsequently applied. In modern imaging pipelines, however, optical systems are increasingly combined with physics-based or learning-based restoration methods, making the information transfer properties of the optical system critically important. In this work, we propose a recovery-oriented optical design approach that explicitly links optical system optimization with image restoration performance through an estimation-theoretic framework based on Fisher information. A new design criterion is adopted to ensure that the information encoded by the optical system can be reliably recovered during image restoration. To validate the proposed approach, two dual separated aspheric lenses are designed under identical configurations using conventional RMS-based optimization and the proposed recovery-oriented optimization, respectively. Although the RMS-optimized lens exhibits superior direct imaging quality, it underperforms after image restoration compared to the recovery-oriented design. These results demonstrate that recovery-oriented optical design provides a physically interpretable and effective extension of traditional optical design criteria for imaging systems operating within modern computational imaging pipelines.

☆ Personalising Deformable Image Registration with Clinical Context and Deformation History for Adaptive Radiotherapy
Caiwen Jiang, Songlin Zhao, Yuzhen Ding, Jia Mi, Samir H. Patel, Alexandra Bennett, Keldon K. Lin, Terence T. Sio, Jonathan B. Ashman, Lisa A. McGee, Jean-Claude M. Rwigema, William G. Rule, Sameer R. Keole, Sujay A. Vora, William W. Wong, Nathan Y. Yu, Michele Y. Halyard, Steven E. Schild, Safia K. Ahmed, Daniel J. Ma, Robert L. Foote, Michelle A. Neben Wittich, Thomas J. Whitaker, Haibo Lin, Dinggang Shen, Wei Liu
Adaptive radiotherapy must account for anatomical changes during treatment, but doing so depends on reliably mapping targets, organs at risk and dose across serial images. Existing registration methods treat each image pair independently, without using radiotherapy-specific context or the patient's preceding anatomical trajectory. We developed Clinical-context-Aware and Patient-adaptive Deformable Image Registration (CAP-DIR), integrating source contours, dose, clinical text and prior-registration features. We evaluated 16,361 CT examinations from 3,473 patients across four institutional cohorts and five public benchmarks. CAP-DIR increased internal-test organ-at-risk-region normalized cross-correlation from 84.76% to 96.92% relative to the strongest learning-based comparator, with low deformation folding, and remained superior across seven external cohorts. In a blinded review of 20 longitudinal cases, clinically acceptable contours increased from 45.0% to 82.5% for clinical target volumes and from 22.5% to 62.5% for organs at risk, while estimated editing time decreased. In a controlled benchmark, CAP-DIR reduced global dose-mapping error by 34.5% relative to the strongest comparator. These findings show that clinically informed, longitudinal registration can improve contour usability and dose mapping for adaptive radiotherapy.

☆ Deficit-Driven Stratified Acquisition for Building STRATA-S12: An Open SAR-Optical Corpus for Self-Supervised Learning
Christian Sanchez-Leon, Dongming Chen, Dongqi Wang
Building a co-registered SAR-optical corpus for self-supervised Earth Observation is above all an acquisition problem, yet the main multi-modal datasets are collected opportunistically, with no per-stratum quota control and no mechanism against the geographic dropout that non-uniform cloud cover leaves behind. We present Deficit-Driven Stratified Acquisition (DDSA), an algorithm that treats building a co-registered Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 corpus as a constrained maximum-coverage problem over a hemisphere-corrected (class x season x region) stratification, enforces strict temporal pairing and a multi-stage quality gate, and closes the loop during acquisition with a human-in-the-loop deficit-repair stage. Measured on its own product, the algorithm yields three results a single-pass acquisition cannot report. Deficit-driven ordering makes a partial run a covering one: it holds every one of the 192 strata populated from the first few percent of the budget, where an abundance-first order leaves most strata empty until the end. Whether a failed attempt can be recovered depends on the temporal persistence of its cause, not the kind of defect: geometric failures such as nodata are among the most repairable (eta = 41.4%) while cloud is among the least (eta = 18.8%), because a cloudy location is cloudy on most dates of its season. The repair loop supplies 39.5% of the released pairs at no measurable quality cost, with 89.8% surviving manual review. The quality guarantee has a price: 2,928,370 acquisition attempts produced 740,746 released pairs. We release the corpus, STRATA-S12, with STAC/PDS4-aligned FAIR sidecars, and a pre-registered linear-probe check confirms it is fit for self-supervised pre-training. A metadata-level coverage comparison against SSL4EO-S12 and SEN12MS situates the corpus over a shared frame; systematic cross-corpus and cross-method comparison is left to follow-up work.

☆ Low-Altitude Agentic Networks: From UAV Connectivity to Workflow-Driven Capability Orchestration
Baolin Chong, Fuhui Zhou, Qihui Wu, Ran Tu
Low-altitude platforms are evolving from connected sensing nodes into autonomous agents capable of bounded task interpretation, skill invocation, and local decision making. Increasing the intelligence of individual unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), however, does not resolve the organization problem that arises when mission workflows depend on capabilities distributed across multiple platforms and provider feasibility changes with network, resource, and mobility conditions. We propose low-altitude agentic networking as a task-level networking paradigm and develop a reference architecture that separates workflow logic from executor identity. Within a validated domain-specific workflow space, each ready operation is translated into a capability requirement and dynamically bound to an agent that remains feasible under current conditions. Task contracts and structured evidence govern workflow execution, while routine provider and link changes are handled through workflow-preserving local adaptation before high-level repair is invoked. A trace-calibrated discrete-event case study identifies a bounded operating region: conventional organization remains effective for simple workflows under stable conditions, whereas agentic networking becomes beneficial when workflow dependencies are tightly coupled, capability feasibility changes during execution, and viable local recovery paths remain available.
☆ Background2Background: a self-supervised background removal framework for high dimensional microscopy
Guangrui Ding, Haonan Lin, Rong Tang, Bethany Weinberg, Jianpeng Ao, Qing Xia, Guorong Hu, Dingcheng Sun, Jiaze Yin, Lei Tian, Ji-Xin Cheng
High-dimensional microscopy captures features across space, time, and spectrum, but complex backgrounds obscure signals. We present Background2Background (B2B), a self-supervised background removal framework leveraging the backgrounds larger correlation relative to the signal. Local pixel shuffling disrupts signal correlations while preserving background structure, transforming signals into effective noise for Noise2Noise-based background removal. Across fluorescence, stimulated Raman scattering and mid-infrared photothermal imaging, B2B achieves over 40-fold background suppression and reveals hidden signatures.
♻ ☆ UEPS: Robust and Efficient MRI Reconstruction
Xiang Zhou, Hong Shang, Zijian Zhan, Tianyu He, Jintao Meng, Dong Liang
Deep unrolled models (DUM) have become the state-of-the-art for accelerated MRI reconstruction, yet their robustness under domain shift remains a critical barrier to clinical adoption. In this work, we identify coil sensitivity map (CSM) estimation as the primary bottleneck limiting generalization. To address this, we propose UEPS, a novel DUM architecture featuring three key designs: (i) an Unrolled Expanded (UE) design that eliminates CSM dependency by reconstructing each coil independently; (ii) progressive resolution, which leverages k-space-to-image mapping for efficient coarse-to-fine refinement; and (iii) sparse attention tailored to MRI's 1D undersampling nature. These physics-grounded designs enable gains in robustness and computational efficiency. We construct a large-scale zero-shot transfer benchmark comprising 10 out-of-distribution (OOD) test sets spanning diverse clinical shifts, anatomy, view, contrast, vendor, field strength, and coil configurations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UEPS consistently and substantially outperforms existing DUM, end-to-end, diffusion, and untrained methods across all OOD tests, achieving state-of-the-art robustness with low-latency inference suitable for real-time deployment.

♻ ☆ Panoramic Out-of-Distribution Segmentation
Mengfei Duan, Yuheng Zhang, Yihong Cao, Fei Teng, Kai Luo, Jiaming Zhang, Kailun Yang, Zhiyong Li
Panoramic imaging enables capturing 360° images with an ultra-wide Field-of-View (FoV) for dense omnidirectional perception, which is critical to applications such as autonomous driving and augmented reality. However, current panoramic semantic segmentation methods fail to identify outliers, and pinhole out-of-distribution segmentation (pinhole-OoS) models perform unsatisfactorily in the panoramic domain due to pixel distortions and background clutter. To address these issues, we introduce a new task, Panoramic Out-of-Distribution Segmentation (PanOoS), with the aim of achieving comprehensive and safe scene understanding. Furthermore, we propose the first solution, POS, which adapts to the characteristics of panoramic images through text-guided prompt distribution learning. The proposed Prompt-based Restoration Attention (PRA) optimizes semantic decoding by prompt guidance and self-adaptive correction, while Bilevel Prompt Distribution Learning (BPDL) refines the manifold of per-pixel mask embeddings via semantic prototype supervision. Besides, to compensate for the scarcity of PanOoS datasets, we establish two benchmarks: DenseOoS, which features diverse outliers in complex environments, and QuadOoS, captured by a quadruped robot with a panoramic annular lens system. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of POS, with AuPRC increasing and FPR95 decreasing by 34.25 and 21.42 percentage points, respectively, compared with RbA on DenseOoS, outperforming state-of-the-art pinhole-OoS methods. Moreover, POS achieves leading closed-set segmentation capabilities and advances the development of panoramic understanding. Code and datasets will be available at https://github.com/MengfeiD/PanOoS.

♻ ☆ Forecasting Brain Tracer Distribution from Pre-Contrast MRI: A Comparison of Direct Regression and Flow Matching
Qinghui Liu, Jon André Ottesen, Thu Nguyen, Geir Ringstad, Ingrid Mossige, Siri Fløgstad Svensson, Atle Bjørnerud, Per Kristian Eide, Kyrre Eeg Emblem
Intrathecal contrast-enhanced MRI shows how a tracer injected into the cerebrospinal fluid spreads through the brain, but requires repeated scans over 24--48\,h. We therefore ask how much of the later tracer distribution can be predicted from the pre-contrast scan and elapsed time alone. Using 104 training patients (878 MRI volumes), we compared a direct image-to-image regression model with a more complex generative model based on conditional flow matching, and tested both on 23 held-out patients and on 51 patients from a separate cohort with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (INPH). The direct model reduced the error of simply copying the pre-contrast scan by about 60\% in held-out patients and 25\% in the INPH cohort, and its predicted change maps agreed with the observed tracer enhancement rather than only reproducing anatomy. The generative model was less accurate in both cohorts. A substantial part of the later tracer distribution is therefore predictable from the patient's brain anatomy as seen on pre-contrast MRI, and the added model complexity gave no benefit at this data scale. With prospective validation, such forecasts could be studied for patient stratification and treatment planning in intrathecal therapies.

☆ Calibrating Generative Flows through Regional Probability Matching
Yubo Huang, Xiongyu Hu, Xin Lai, Zixi Wang, Liao Jian, Jingzehua Xu, Chuan He
Generative models offer a powerful route to scientific simulation and discovery by enabling the study of complex populations and rare phenomena. Flow matching can generate realistic samples, yet inaccurate occurrence frequencies can distort population statistics and compromise inferences about rare events. Here we developed generalized mass-preserving coupled flow matching (G-MPCF), which matches the probability masses of Gaussian source regions to those of weighted data regions. This construction encodes the desired regional frequencies in the correspondence between noise and observations, shaping the learned dynamics while preserving the prescribed target distribution. On a rare-mode benchmark, G-MPCF reduces relative score error by 95.0% and numerical integration error by 89.9% compared with independent flow matching. On CIFAR-10 with a 100:1 class-probability ratio, it reduces corrected class-mass error by 44.6% compared with minibatch optimal transport, while improving mean image fidelity with matched computational budgets. We envision that incorporating regional probability calibration into generative modelling will support more reliable scientific simulation and inference, enabling the study of systems in which rare events and their occurrence frequencies are central to understanding the underlying mechanisms.

♻ ☆ Learned Hemodynamic Coupling Inference in Resting-State Functional MRI
William Consagra, Eardi Lila
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) provides an indirect measurement of neuronal activity via hemodynamic responses that vary across brain regions and individuals. Ignoring this hemodynamic variability can bias downstream connectivity estimates. Furthermore, the hemodynamic parameters themselves may serve as important imaging biomarkers. Estimating spatially varying hemodynamics from resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) is therefore an important but challenging blind inverse problem, since both the latent neural activity and the hemodynamic coupling are unknown. In this work, we propose a methodology for inferring hemodynamic coupling on the cortical surface from rsfMRI. Our approach avoids the highly unstable joint recovery of neural activity and hemodynamics by marginalizing out the latent neural signal and basing inference on the resulting marginal likelihood. To enable scalable, high-resolution estimation, we employ a deep neural network combined with conditional normalizing flows to accurately approximate this intractable marginal likelihood, while enforcing spatial coherence through priors defined on the cortical surface that admit sparse representations. Uncertainty in the hemodynamic estimates is quantified via a double-bootstrap procedure. The proposed approach is extensively validated using synthetic data and real fMRI datasets, demonstrating clear improvements over current methods for hemodynamic estimation and downstream connectivity reproducibility.

Filippo Bragato, Michael Neri, Paolo Testolina, Marco Giordani, Federica Battisti
In recent years, the development of interconnected devices has expanded in many fields, from infotainment to education and industrial applications. This trend has been accelerated by the increased number of low-cost sensors and accessibility to powerful hardware and software. One area that significantly benefits from these advancements is Teleoperated Driving. In this scenario, a remote controller (human or software) safely drives a vehicle using sensor data generated onboard the vehicle, and exchanged via Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications. In this work, we tackle the problem of detecting the presence of cars, pedestrians, and cyclists from point cloud data generated by LiDAR sensors to enable safe Teleoperated Driving operations. Specifically, we use the SELMA dataset, a multimodal, open-source, synthetic dataset for autonomous driving, that we expanded by including the ground-truth bounding boxes of 3D objects to support object detection. Finally, we measure the impact of compression and detection on a simulated V2X network in terms of data rate and latency with respect to the 3GPP requirements of Teleoperated Driving applications. Our results show that G-PCC outperforms its competitors in terms of both compression efficiency and accuracy, and consumes fewer channel resources for data transmissions. On the contrary, the two most conservative quantization modes of Draco, combined with SECOND or PointPillars for object detection, offer superior speed in both compression and decompression with comparable accuracy. Finally, we show that the choice of the detector depends on the class of objects to detect, specifically pedestrians or cyclists.

♻ ☆ Multimodal synthesis of MRI and tabular data with diffusion in a joint latent space via cross-attention
Daniel Mensing, Jan Kapar, Jochen G. Hirsch, Matthias Günther, Horst Hahn, Marvin N. Wright

Our model utilizes a variational autoencoder to fuse the two modalities before diffusion-based synthesis, allowing modality-appropriate reconstruction with separate decoders for MRI and tabular data. We evaluated the framework on data from the German National Cohort (NAKO Gesundheitsstudie), comprising over 10,000 participants with MRI scans and clinical tabular features such as age, sex, body measurements, and ethnicity. In the tabular modality, our model outperformed CTGAN across standard evaluation metrics and achieved results comparable to TVAE, demonstrating competitive performance relative to established unimodal baselines. This work is, to our knowledge, the first to demonstrate the feasibility of jointly modeling MRI and mixed-type tabular data in a single latent diffusion framework, offering a proof-of-concept for generating coherent synthetic multimodal patient data and aligning with the broader goal of developing digital twins in healthcare.
♻ ☆ GS-DOT: Gaussian splatting-based image reconstruction for diffuse optical tomography
Jingjing Jiang
This work presents GS-DOT, a novel image reconstruction framework based on Gaussian Splatting (GS) for diffuse optical tomography (DOT). Inspired by GS for rendering applications, absorption coefficients are represented as a sparse sum of anisotropic Gaussian primitives optimized to fit measured time-resolved point-spread functions through analytic gradients and Adam optimization. This is the first adaptation of GS algorithms in the photon diffusion regime, where the ray transport function is replaced by the diffusion functions to enable accurate modeling of light transport in highly scattering media. Validation on synthetic tissue models demonstrate high accuracy in localization and quantification of reconstructed absorption maps for both clean and noisy signals. GS-DOT has demonstrated high robustness to noise and showed a huge reduction in memory demand.

Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) is essential for embodied perception, where panoramic cameras provide a 360° field of view to reduce blind spots and keep surrounding targets observable for longer durations. In videos represented in equirectangular projection (ERP), horizontal coordinates wrap at the image seam, while frame-wise relative-depth estimates may fluctuate over time. Furthermore, a Topology-Aware Cylindrical Motion Model (TCMM) lifts horizontal motion into a continuous angular state space, enabling seam-consistent motion prediction and association. By jointly modeling trajectory-level depth consistency and panoramic topology, CylindTrack improves identity preservation and trajectory continuity in challenging panoramic scenes. Experiments on QuadTrack and JRDB demonstrate improvements in identity-oriented metrics with practical efficiency, achieving HOTA scores of 33.67 and 31.12, IDF1 scores of 40.45 and 34.33, and tracking speeds of 28.56 and 21.34 FPS, respectively. The source code will be released at https://github.com/warriordby/CylindTrack.

♻ ☆ Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Cardiac Segmentation: Towards Structure Mutual Information Maximization CVPR
Changjie Lu, Shen Zheng, Gaurav Gupta
Unsupervised domain adaptation approaches have recently succeeded in various medical image segmentation tasks. The reported works often tackle the domain shift problem by aligning the domain-invariant features and minimizing the domain-specific discrepancies. That strategy works well when the difference between a specific domain and between different domains is slight. However, the generalization ability of these models on diverse imaging modalities remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces UDA-VAE++, an unsupervised domain adaptation framework for cardiac segmentation. We show that the evidence lower bound of VAE-based domain adaptation penalizes the mutual information between the image and the latent space, including the structure information that segmentation relies on. Maximizing the structure mutual information removes this penalty on the structure information, while the remaining information is still compressed. To estimate this term, we develop a novel Structure Mutual Information Estimation (SMIE) block with a global estimator, a local estimator, and a prior information matching estimator to maximize the mutual information between the reconstruction and segmentation tasks. Specifically, we design a novel sequential reparameterization scheme that enables information flow and variance correction from the low-resolution latent space to the high-resolution latent space. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark cardiac segmentation datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms previous state-of-the-art qualitatively and quantitatively. The code is available at https://github.com/LOUEY233/Toward-Mutual-Information

♻ ☆ Efficient Test-Time Adaptation through Latent Subspace Coefficients Search
Xinyu Luo, Jie Liu, Kecheng Chen, Yihua Shao, Junyi Yang, Bo Ding, Nicu Sebe, Arindam Basu, Haoliang Li
Real-world deployment often exposes vision models to distribution shifts, making test-time adaptation (TTA) important for reliable prediction. Existing TTA methods can be difficult to deploy on edge devices because they require backpropagation, activation storage, or test-time batches, which increase computation, memory, and state. ELaTTA freezes the pretrained model and adapts each test input by searching a low-dimensional coefficient vector in a principal latent subspace computed offline from a source-domain cache. The basis is stored once and source data are discarded before deployment. At test time, CMA-ES performs covariance-adaptive Gaussian search, ranks candidate corrections by prediction entropy, and selects the best candidate within a fixed evaluation budget. On five visual benchmarks spanning corruption, natural, rendition, sketch, and cross-domain shifts, ELaTTA provides strong accuracy under strict and continual single-instance protocols. In the strict single-instance comparison, MEMO requires \emph{64.7$\times$} the computation and \emph{12.4$\times$} the peak memory of ELaTTA. A complementary keyword-spotting experiment shows that the same coefficient-search design transfers beyond vision. We further demonstrate ViT-Base adaptation on a Raspberry Pi 5, confirming the feasibility of deploying ELaTTA on an edge device.

☆ Jensen-Bregman split Gibbs sampling

Because the family contains the DFT and the DCT-IV (a variant of the DCT) as exact points, training can start from these transforms, and it improves on its starting point at the compression level it is trained for. We evaluate the bases on natural photographs and line drawings. On photographs, which the cosine basis already fits well, the best trained basis leads the DCT only under aggressive truncation. On Quick Draw line drawings, under a common codec at matched quality, the best trained basis stores each image in about 20% fewer bytes than the 8x8 block cosine transform of the Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) format, not counting the one-off storage of the basis.

☆ Frozen Site-Probe Accuracy Is Not a Standalone Harmonization Score: An Audit of Evaluation Practice for Multi-Site MRI
Muhammad Muqsit Islam, Gloria García Cuenco, José M. Martínez, Pierrick Coupé
Image-level MRI harmonization is often evaluated with a frozen site probe, a site classifier trained on raw scans and applied unchanged to harmonized ones: a drop in its accuracy is read as removal of site effects. We audit this practice on ABIDE I (1,112 T1-weighted scans, 17 sites) with ten output sets from seven harmonization methods and controls for chance, head shape, intensity, preprocessing and target alignment. We find that this verdict depends on how the probe is trained, even among probes that classify raw scans well: across random seeds, its balanced accuracy on the same CycleGAN outputs ranges from 0.13 to 0.59 (chance: 0.06). Low frozen-probe accuracy can also arise without harmonization: a Gaussian blur, which increases the intensity distance to the target site, lowers this accuracy to chance. Moreover, where the frozen probe fails, probes trained on the harmonized scans still recover the site, even from intensity histograms alone: on HACA3 outputs, the frozen probe scores 0.25, a probe trained on those outputs 0.75, and one using only their intensity histograms 0.71. Low frozen-probe accuracy therefore does not show that site information has been removed. We recommend reporting several probes trained to convergence, probes trained on harmonized scans, and target alignment.

☆ Model-agnostic Knowledge Augmented Machine Learning for Weakly Annotated Bioimaging Data
Jayanie Bogahawatte, Sachith Seneviratne, Simon Maksour, Dzung Do-Ha, Elizabeth Qian, Samuel Brennan, Matthew Keon, Lezanne Ooi, Saman Halgamuge
Machine learning models are increasingly used for automated feature extraction from weakly annotated bioimaging data, such as microscopy and cytomorphology images. Due to the sole dependency of automated feature extraction, existing methods yield inconsistent classification performance across weakly annotated datasets. Here, we propose a model-agnostic knowledge augmentation method that enables ML models to exploit domain knowledge beyond what automated feature extraction can capture. The proposed approach improves classification performance across seven ML architectures. When integrated with masked autoencoder-based self-supervised learning, our method achieves the strongest overall performance, improving precision by 2.9% over the next-best method on three in-house microscopy datasets and by an average of 6.8% across three public cytomorphology benchmarks. We perform nucleus-level classification based on mislocalization of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, a phenotype linked to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), using three independent microscopy datasets of motor neurons derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells. Accurate quantification of this phenotype at scale remains challenging and may contribute to inconsistencies across studies. Application of the best-performing model to these microscopy datasets reveals biological interpretations related to ALS, including dose-dependent effects of the proteasomal stressor, MG132, and the oxidative stressor, sodium arsenite (SA), on TDP-43 mislocalization, variable pathology in motor neurons from sporadic and familial ALS donors, and a lack of protection of the pharmacological compounds, edaravone and niclosamide, against SA-induced TDP-43 mislocalization. Together, our pipeline enables in-vitro cellular image analysis to advance understanding of ALS-associated pathology and potential treatments.
☆ Exploring the Latent Structure of AMD Severity Using Retinal Foundation Models
Niccolò Fineschi, Jovana Panic, Atsushi Watanabe, Hideaki Hayashi, Kazuya Nishimura, Yuki Maeno, Samanta Rosati, Gabriella Balestra, Kohji Nishida, Hajime Nagahara
Retinal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of ophthalmic tasks, yet relatively little is known about how disease-related information is represented within their learned embeddings and whether this distribution influences downstream prediction performance. In this work, we use Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) as a case study to investigate how disease severity is represented within the embedding space of RET-CLIP, a retinal vision-language foundation model, using bilateral fundus images from the AREDS dataset, benchmarked against non-retinal encoders. We first characterize the distribution of AMD severity within the learned representation space and then evaluate how this structure influences classification performance across three clinically relevant task formulations of increasing granularity. Finally, we analyze the most influential latent dimensions combining feature attribution, statistical phenotype association, and qualitative image analyses. Our results show that RET-CLIP represents AMD severity as a continuous spectrum rather than a set of discrete categories, with healthy and advanced disease stages exhibiting clearer separation than intermediate ones. This organization was reflected in downstream performance, which decreased from a balanced accuracy of 0.844 and 0.814 for binary AMD and Late-AMD detection respectively to 0.446 for six-class grading. Furthermore, the most influential latent dimensions were statistically associated to distinct retinal phenotypes, including drusen accumulation, pigmentary alterations, and advanced retinal lesions. These findings suggest that the structure of retinal foundation-model representations influences the difficulty of clinically relevant prediction tasks and demonstrate the potential of representation-level analysis for understanding disease organization and improving interpretability.

☆ Desertification Forecasting in Semi-Arid Regions: Using Deep Learning to Probe the Observability Limits of Land Degradation Dynamics
Filipe Moura Da Silva, Cláubio Landney Lima Bandeira
Forecasting desertification has received far less attention than mapping it. We use a convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) trained on ten annual Earth Observation (EO) variables (2000-2023) over the semi-arid state of Ceará, Brazil, on a 256x206 grid at roughly 2.2 km resolution, to measure how much of the year-to-year evolution of a MapBiomas-derived degradation index (IDV) can be predicted from satellite data. The network predicts a bounded change on top of the last observed state, is trained in two stages (single-step, then recursive rollout) and is evaluated on a contiguous spatial and temporal holdout. State-wide mean IDV rose from 0.238 to 0.350 between 2000 and 2023, about 0.005 per year, but cell-level change is dominated by year-to-year jumps, and a gradient-boosting model given all channels explains only 4.7% of its variance. Against this ceiling, the ConvLSTM lowers RMSE relative to persistence by 1.6% one year ahead and 4.4% four years ahead in a held-out southern band (p < 0.001), beats persistence with a constant drift and reproduces 53-69% of the regional drift. Drift-aware baselines only help from the third year onward, by up to 4.4% in RMSE at six years. An earlier formulation that redrew the whole field each year predicted changes unrelated to the observed ones (correlation -0.06) and produced a spurious decline when run recursively. Channel knockouts suggest that elevation and EVI degrade the forecast, while slope and aspect have no measurable effect. Monte Carlo dropout and stochastic scenario maps convey the uncertainty that the expected-value forecast hides. Under climatological forcing, mean IDV rises from 0.350 in 2023 to 0.370 in 2030. EO-based desertification forecasting is therefore reliable for the regional trend, not for individual cells.

☆ Radiomics-Based Thyroid Nodule Classification with Label-Conditional Conformal Prediction
Laura Testa, Pierpaolo Brutti, Umberto Ferraro Petrillo
Thyroid nodule malignancy assessment relies on ultrasound imaging, yet current risk stratification systems suffer from substantial interobserver variability, contributing to a high rate of unnecessary biopsies. We propose a radiomics-based framework combining quantitative feature extraction via PyRadiomics with a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) classifier, selected among six candidates for its favorable trade-off between discriminative performance and interpretability. To complement point predictions with uncertainty estimates, Cross-Conformal Prediction with label-conditional guarantees is applied, flagging ambiguous cases for clinical review rather than forcing a binary decision. Experiments are conducted on TN5000, a publicly available ultrasound dataset of thyroid nodules. After Spearman correlation filtering, 36 features are retained and the GAM achieves an AUC of $0.89$, a sensitivity of $0.83$, and a specificity of $0.82$ on the validation set. At a significance level $ε=0.09$, selected to ensure empirical coverage guarantees on both classes, 63\% of nodules on the test set receive a certain (i.e., single-label) prediction, with conditional precision of $0.94$ for certain malignant and conditional Negative Predictive Value (NPV) of $0.73$ for certain benign cases, while the remaining 37\% are referred to the clinician.

☆ The Predictability Bias of Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning in Medical Imaging
Fabian Drexel, Bernhard Kainz, Jakob N. Kather, Daniel Rueckert, Lisa C. Adams, Keno K. Bressem, Cosmin I. Bercea
Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn by predicting teacher representations of masked regions from visible context. Point prediction summarizes the conditional target distribution and cannot reproduce variation that the context does not resolve. We call this constraint predictability bias. In computed tomography (CT), recurrent anatomy is predictable from context, whereas the sporadic, localized pathology that determines clinical interpretation often is not. We introduce TAP-JEPA, a ViT-B/3D trained on 113,611 CT volumes that is competitive with state-of-the-art encoders (COLIPRI, Merlin, VoxelFM) in scan-level classification. We then audit the learned predictive pathway by replaying the exact masking, teacher, and predictor computations used during training. Prediction lowers the mean Skill (prevalence-normalized average precision) from 0.388 to 0.271 for pathology, but only from 0.921 to 0.873 for anatomy. Along the teacher direction, separating pathology from matched control regions in the same organ, prediction moves pathology 34.7% toward the controls and controls 13.6% toward pathology, with larger shifts farther from visible context. Replacing visible matched-control representations increases surrounding-target prediction loss more than fully replacing pathology representations across four pathology categories. Downstream, removing all final-layer pathology tokens reduces the decision margin by at most 0.45% in four of seven scan-level probes. Together, these results show that contextual predictability is not a sufficient proxy for clinical relevance in medical representation learning. Training objectives should therefore retain diagnostic features regardless of their predictability from surrounding anatomy.

☆ Stochastic Finite-Transition Learning and Exploration for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
Muhammad Usama Mirza, Esin Öztürk Işık, Tolga Çukur
Generative MRI reconstruction maps an initial source distribution to the target image distribution along a learned recovery trajectory. Common generative methods, such as diffusion and flow, typically learn fine-grained local dynamics whose integration defines this global mapping, hence requiring many network evaluations at inference. Existing few-step sampling approaches can lower computational burden by approximating large transformations from local dynamics, albeit at the expense of reconstruction fidelity. FLEX-MRI instead partitions recovery into a small number of finite intervals between retained states defined by progressive changes in k-space support, and directly learns the reconstruction change across each interval. Because such finite transitions can admit multiple plausible outcomes, FLEX-MRI combines support-relaxed finite-transition learning with stochastic exploration. During training, randomized k-space sampling masks define finite-transition targets with varying support, while the prediction loss remains unrestricted by each individual mask. At inference, FLEX-MRI perturbs a random subset of currently estimated k-space coefficients, allowing the learned predictor to stochastically explore alternative transition paths. Each predicted state is then reconciled with the acquired measurements through data consistency. We theoretically show that this stochastic exploration induces nonzero transition-level variation through the learned recovery map and data consistency without requiring an auxiliary generative sampler. Experiments on multi-coil MRI datasets show that FLEX-MRI outperforms competing methods while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to few-step baselines.
♻ ☆ Compression Hurts, Pooling Helps: Information Loss in Rayleigh-Scale Estimation from B-Mode Ultrasound
D. Hudson Smith, Ahmer Raza
Clinical B-mode images are widely available as potential data sources for quantitative ultrasound (QUS) analysis for tissue characterization. However, standard clinical ultrasound devices apply unknown log-compression to RF envelope data before display and storage. Previous work has demonstrated estimation of the underlying RF envelope statistics in the presence of an unknown compression law. Using Fisher information analysis, we show that finite-offset log compression causes severe information loss when estimating the Rayleigh scale $σ$, which controls diffuse speckle. For a single image window, unknown compression raises the minimum achievable variance for unbiased estimation of $σ$ by a compression-independent factor of approximately 34.98. When $M$ equal-sized windows share the same unknown compression settings, the excess variance decays as $1/M$; even in the most favorable regime, reducing the variance inflation factor below 1.1 requires 340 windows. Our analysis treats the contrast parameter $a$ as unknown and the boundary offset $b$ as known; estimating $b$ experimentally shows even larger variance. We validate this theory using synthetic estimation experiments and demonstrate RF-scale recovery on real RF-envelope windows from the OASBUD dataset. Together, these results clarify the limitations of using routine B-mode images for QUS.

♻ ☆ Scale-specific auxiliary multi-task contrastive learning for deep liver vessel segmentation
Amine Sadikine, Bogdan Badic, Jean-Pierre Tasu, Vincent Noblet, Pascal Ballet, Dimitris Visvikis, Pierre-Henri Conze
Extracting hepatic vessels from abdominal images is of high interest for clinicians since it allows to divide the liver into functionally-independent Couinaud segments. In this respect, an automated liver blood vessel extraction is widely summoned. Despite the significant growth in performance of semantic segmentation methodologies, preserving the complex multi-scale geometry of main vessels and ramifications remains a major challenge. This paper provides a new deep supervised approach for vessel segmentation, with a strong focus on representations arising from the different scales inherent to the vascular tree geometry. In particular, we propose a new clustering technique to decompose the tree into various scale levels, from tiny to large vessels. Then, we extend standard 3D UNet to multi-task learning by incorporating scale-specific auxiliary tasks and contrastive learning to encourage the discrimination between scales in the shared representation. Promising results, depicted in several evaluation metrics, are revealed on the public 3D-IRCADb dataset.

♻ ☆ Multiclass histogram-based thresholding using kernel density estimation and scale-space representations
S. Korneev, J. Gilles, I. Battiato
We present a method for multiclass thresholding of histograms whose modes may overlap so strongly that they merge into a unimodal distribution. The histogram is approximated by a nonparametric kernel density (KD) estimate, a mixture of Gaussians with one component per bin and a common bandwidth, whose parameters are determined by Expectation-Maximization (EM) iterations. Because the estimate is a Gaussian mixture, the semigroup property of Gaussian convolution yields its scale-space representation in closed form, at bandwidths both larger and smaller than the fitted one. The algorithm increases or decreases the bandwidth until the number of local minima of the estimate equals the number of requested classes minus one, and returns the positions of those minima as the threshold values. We validate the method on synthetic histograms with known thresholds, and we apply it to the histogram of X-ray computed tomography images of a natural porous sample in which the three phases strongly overlap. The porosity computed from the resulting segmentation agrees with the direct experimental measurement to within 4%, whereas K-means clustering misestimates it by 52%.
♻ ☆ Leveraging Motion Estimation for Efficient Bayer-Domain Video Convolutional Networks
Haichao Wang, Jiangtao Wen, Yuxing Han
Existing computer vision pipelines suffer from two efficiency bottlenecks: image signal processors (ISPs) first convert Bayer pixel data to RGB pixel by pixel, and video models repeatedly process temporally redundant frames, leading to high power consumption and latency. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that eliminates the ISP and leverages motion estimation to accelerate video vision tasks directly in the Bayer domain. We introduce Motion Estimation-based Video Convolution (MEVC), which integrates sliding-window motion estimation into each convolutional layer, enabling prediction and residual-based refinement that reduces redundant computations across frames. This design bridges the structural gap between block-based motion estimation and spatial convolution, enabling accurate, low-cost processing. Our end-to-end pipeline supports raw Bayer input and achieves over 70% reduction in FLOPs with minimal accuracy degradation across video semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and object detection benchmarks, using both synthetic Bayer-converted and real Bayer video datasets.
♻ ☆ Selective Depthwise Separable Convolution for Lightweight Joint Source-Channel Coding in Wireless Image Transmission
Ming Ye, Kui Cai, Cunhua Pan, Zhen Mei, Wanting Yang, Chunguo Li
Depthwise separable convolutional (DSConv) layers have been successfully applied to deep learning (DL)-based joint source-channel coding (JSCC) schemes to reduce computational complexity. However, a systematic investigation of the layerwise and ratio-wise replacement of standard convolutional (Conv) layers with DSConv layers in JSCC systems for wireless image transmission remains largely unexplored. In this letter, we propose a configurable lightweight JSCC framework that incorporates a selective replacement strategy, enabling flexible Conv-to-DSConv replacement at different replacement ratios and positions. By varying the replacement ratio, we obtain models with different computational complexities and analyze their impact on reconstruction performance. Furthermore, we investigate how replacements at different encoder and decoder depths influence reconstruction quality under a fixed replacement ratio. Our results show that Conv-to-DSConv replacement at the intermediate layers of the encoder and decoder achieves a favorable complexity-performance trade-off, revealing layer-wise redundancy in DL-based JSCC systems. Extensive experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves substantial parameter reduction with only slight performance degradation, enabling flexible complexity-performance trade-offs for resource-constrained edge devices.
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures, journal
♻ ☆ One-Bin Fourier Challenges for Dimension-Free Reconstruction Certification
Milad Bafarassat
Partial-Fourier measurement underlies computational imaging, and its reconstructions increasingly come from iterative or learned solvers whose recovery guarantees are conditional on a signal model, a sampling law, and solver accuracy. None of those guarantees transfers to a particular committed output: it can satisfy every acquired coefficient while remaining badly wrong in the unmeasured nullspace. Native Fourier holdout does not repair this, since a spectrally concentrated error is missed unless its bin is drawn, so uniform worst-case risk needs a number of hidden bins proportional to the dimension. We propose a post-commit acceptance test: secret finite-phase masks turn one fixed Fourier readout into dense randomized residual checks, and a median-of-means threshold handles calibrated readout noise. We prove that errors above $E_{\rm rej}$ are rejected and errors below $E_{\rm acc}$ are accepted with confidence $1-δ$ once $q\ge C(1+Nσ^2/E_{\rm rej})^2\log(1/δ)$, explicitly exposing the one-bin resolution floor $Nσ^2/\sqrt q$; in the zero-noise limit, QPSK gives $4^{-q}$ soundness versus $97.9\%$ minimax false acceptance for a worst-case ordinary-bin error. At a fixed noise-to-threshold ratio, measured screening false acceptance fell from about $21\%$ at 16 checks to $5\%$ at 64; a data-consistent learned nullspace failure with NMSE $0.200$ was rejected by $96.9\%$ of challenge banks while 16 ordinary bins missed it $98.9\%$ of the time; and error statistics at 16 checks stayed stable from 128 through $65{,}536$ dimensions. The test supports solver acceptance, model selection, and stopping certification, with a certified fresh-bank error interval.
comment: The author withdraws this paper because the coded-diffraction implementation claimed in Section 3.3 is not established. The certification procedure requires complex-valued linear Fourier measurements, whereas intensity-only acquisition does not directly provide them. The manuscript does not establish the additional acquisition procedure needed to bridge this gap
♻ ☆ Low, High, and Semantic-Level Vision-Language Learning for AI-Generated Image Detection
Qian Yao, Luming Yang, Jun-Jie Huang, Yongjun Wang, Xinwang Liu, Meng Wang
Driven by advances in diffusion models and autoregressive models, the fidelity and resolution of AI-generated images now rival those of real images. However, existing AI-generated image detection methods often downsample the images,inevitably overlooking critical low-level texture details in high-resolution AI-generated images, thereby limiting their detection performance. In addition, the continuous emergence of unknown generative models makes large-scale pre-training datasets inaccessible. To address these challenges, we propose a novel AI-generated image detector, termed LHSDet (Low-, High-, and Semantic-level Detection). Specifically, we formulate the AI-generated image detection task as a Visual Question Answering problem, leveraging a fine-tuned vision-language framework to fully exploit the complementary information between visual and textual modalities. Recognizing that the default visual encoder of existing vision-language models is not tailored for AI-generated image detection, we redesign a visual encoder to better capture both the low-level and high-level artifacts inherent in AI-generated images. Furthermore, we incorporate a semantic-level textual branch to enable multi-modal feature fusion and detection. Consequently, LHSDet employs a triple-branch architecture to extract complementary multi-modal features: a low-level visual branch that aggregates non-overlapping patches for local texture cues, a high-level visual branch based on SigLIP2 for global perception feature extraction,and a semantic-level textual branch that generates captions using BLIP-2. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that LHSDet achieves strong detection accuracy and robust performance across diverse generative models.
